title: Yes, No, Please and Thank You
description: The small words that carry every exchange at a counter or a table: the Sanaa yes إي, no, please, thanks and its reply, sorry, okay — and the God-phrases that punctuate every sentence whoever is speaking.
approach: GPA Phase 1 — receptive first, then the first tiny productions: a learner can say إي, لا and شكراً within minutes. Politeness particles are taught with their expected replies.
can_do: Say yes, no, please and thank you and answer thanks
Apologise and get someone's attention politely
Use the everyday religious phrases everyone uses

grammar.title: Noticing: God-phrases are grammar
grammar.explanation: In Yemen إن شاء الله, الحمد لله and ما شاء الله are not signs of piety; they are the ordinary way of talking about the future, the present and something admirable. Ask a shopkeeper if he has bread tomorrow and the yes is إن شاء الله. Say you are fine and it is الحمد لله. Praise someone's baby without ما شاء الله and an older relative may quietly add it for you. Nothing to memorise beyond the phrases themselves — just notice where they fall in a sentence.

examples.english: The bread is good, God be praised

culture.title: God-phrases everyone uses
culture.note: Whatever a Yemeni's own religiosity, these phrases are how the language is spoken. إن شاء الله answers any question about the future, from 'will you come?' to 'is the bus at nine?' — and it can mean a warm yes or a gentle probably-not, which you learn to read from the tone. الحمد لله answers 'how are you', ends a meal and greets good news. ما شاء الله is what you say about a child, a car, a house, anything admirable, to keep the evil eye off it. Use them freely: nobody will ever think you are pretending.

phrases.english: What God wills (said of something admirable)
Thank God for your safe arrival

culture.title: Thanks and its reply
culture.note: شكراً is fine, but Yemenis thank each other with blessings more often than with the plain word: تسلم 'may you be kept safe', الله يبارك فيك 'may God bless you', يعطيك العافية to anyone who has done work. The reply to any of these is العفو, or a blessing back. Refusing tea or coffee politely takes لا شكراً with the right hand on the chest — and expect to be offered twice more.

phrases.english: Thank you, my friend (lit. may you be safe)
No thank you, God keep you

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Sanaa yes — a short, clean ii with a stop in front of it, by far the commonest form in the highlands. ايوه and نعم are also heard everywhere and are safe. The trap is the MSA-only نعم as your only yes: say إي and you sound local.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man nodding once with a raised thumb, plain background.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any short yes in a sketch or interview; listen for the clipped إي.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Same everywhere in Arabic. Yemenis soften it with a blessing (لا، الله يسلمك) or with a raised hand and a click of the tongue. On its own it also means 'don't' before a verb, which you will meet later.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man shaking his head, palm raised gently, plain background.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any refusal; a vendor or host being told no.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'If you permit' — the please of requests: هات مي لو سمحت. To a woman, لو سمحتي. من فضلك is understood but sounds bookish in Yemen; لو سمحت is what people say.
vocabulary.image_scene: A customer at a shop counter pointing at bread with a polite open hand.
vocabulary.video_hint: Ordering at a stall or café; asking a stranger something.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Understood everywhere and always polite, though Yemenis more often thank with a blessing — تسلم, الله يبارك فيك, مشكور. Learn شكراً first, collect the blessings as you hear them.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman receiving a tea glass with her right hand, smiling in thanks.
vocabulary.video_hint: Thanks said at a counter or on receiving something; the reply usually follows.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The standard reply to thanks — 'it is nothing to forgive'. Also heard as عفواً. A blessing back (الله يسلمك) does the same job.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopkeeper waving a hand dismissively with a warm smile, as if to say it was nothing.
vocabulary.video_hint: The reply right after شكراً in any exchange.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A man says آسف, a woman آسفة. For a small bump or slip, Yemenis more often say معليش — 'never mind' — which works both as an apology and as forgiveness.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man with a hand on his chest and an apologetic tilt of the head after knocking over a tea glass.
vocabulary.video_hint: An apology in a sketch — a spill, a late arrival.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'Allow me' — how you stop a stranger to ask a question or squeeze past in a crowded souq. Often preceded by a vocative: يا أخي اسمح لي. To a woman: اسمحي لي.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man in a busy souq lane touching his chest and leaning toward a vendor to ask something.

example.english: Excuse me, where is the mosque?

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone stopping a passer-by; the moment before a question in street footage.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The most-used okay in Yemen — 'good, alright, well then'. Shortened to طب at the start of a sentence. The ط is voiced in Sanaa, so it sounds close to 'dayyib' to an English ear; that is normal.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man giving a small nod and an open palm, as if agreeing to a plan.
vocabulary.video_hint: Agreement in a conversation; the word that closes a plan.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'Naturally.' أكيد 'certainly' does the same job and is just as common. Both are answers to 'can I…?' and 'is it…?'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A host spreading both hands wide with an of-course expression.
vocabulary.video_hint: An emphatic yes to a request.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Attaches to anything in the future. Also the softest possible way to say no — a vague إن شاء الله to a request is a maybe at best. Written as one word انشالله online.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man looking upward with a hopeful smile, one hand raised palm-up.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any mention of tomorrow or a plan; the phrase almost always follows.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The answer to how are you, the word after a meal, the response to good news and — with a shrug — to bad news too. The ll of الله is dark and held.
vocabulary.image_scene: A family finishing a meal, the father leaning back with both palms up in thanks.
vocabulary.video_hint: After كيف حالك; at the end of a meal in cooking vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'There is no problem' — Yemeni ما فيش, spoken as two words, with the Sanaa alternative مابش. عادي 'normal, no big deal' is the one-word version. Never the Egyptian مفيش.
vocabulary.image_scene: A mechanic wiping his hands and waving off a worried customer with a relaxed smile.
vocabulary.video_hint: Reassurance after an apology or a hitch; مابش/ما فيش audible.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.english: Tea? No, sorry, there isn't any

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.english: You're welcome — you're always welcome here

sound_spotlight.explanation: ح is the deep breathy h; ه is the ordinary one. الحمد has the deep one, لله the light one — both in one phrase you say twenty times a day.
The double l of الله is pronounced with the back of the tongue raised, thicker than an English l, and held. Every God-phrase carries it.
Yemeni negation ends in a sharp -sh. Hear it at the end of فيش now; later it will attach to verbs too.

lesson_sequence.detail: A bread stall at the edge of the souq. One line of English: these are the small words that carry every purchase and every table.
Twelve cards, illustration and native audio, Arabic large, no English.
Three call-and-reply pairs replayed as mini scenes: please/thanks/you're welcome, sorry/no problem, question/إن شاء الله.
Audio only, four-image grid, all twelve.
Record إي, لا and شكراً; compare with native audio. No scoring beyond a play-back.
Counter rolls up. Nudge: say الحمد لله after your next meal.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you buy anything, say لو سمحت when you ask and شكراً when you get it — and listen for the reply.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Two productions with a guaranteed feedback loop.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Count how many times you hear إن شاء الله in your next conversation with a Yemeni. Was any of them really a no?
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification. Trains pragmatic listening on the most-used phrase in the language.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tell your tutor something admirable about their city and see if they wait for your ما شاء الله.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor prompt. Practises the phrase in its real social slot.

video_needs.scene: Short exchanges at a shop counter or table: thanks and the reply, an apology, an okay, the vendor's إي and إن شاء الله.
